job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Carla Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my grandmother in a village outside Debrecen, and I catch the 6:50 bus to the university. I'm doing a master's in automation engineering, so days are lectures on control systems and time in the lab with a conveyor model we're building. Evenings I help with my mum's vegetables and in autumn the apple harvest. On Sundays I sing in the church choir. Last summer I spent six weeks at a car wiring factory, shadowing the maintenance team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because most of the fuss was noise. At church or at home I'd say work is still work: someone has to keep a factory running and someone has to grow the food. I wouldn't post anything online, because I don't use it for opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. Automation engineers still get called at night when a line stops, and that's a human job. I owe about twelve thousand in loans and I haven't got an offer, but the factories around here do take graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to the three factories within an hour's bus ride and ask my old maintenance supervisor, Mr Szabo, for a word. I'd keep helping at home with the orchard. I wouldn't use any AI tools, because I'd rather learn the machine myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. I live at home, I have my family and my work is something real. I do worry a bit about the first job, but not more than any graduate does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think automation engineers stay needed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when a drive fails at two in the morning, you need someone who understands the cables and the logic. A program can suggest, but it can't stand in the plant with a torch. At least that's how it looked in the factory where I worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your family say about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother says I should have a job in the village and marry a good man. I'd say job first. But I'd like to stay near home, so I'd look at the local plants before anything in Budapest.

say: I'd say work is still work: someone keeps the **factory running**, someone grows the food.
think: Automation engineers still get called at **night** when a line stops.
I owe about **twelve thousand** and have no offer, but local factories hire.
do: Finish the master's and apply to **three factories** within an hour's bus ride.
Ask Mr Szabo at the car wiring factory for a **word**.
feel: I feel **calm enough**, with my family and real work around me.
S0.quote: When a drive fails at two in the morning, you need someone who understands the cables and the logic.
fieldNote: Carla is **calm** because the work is physical, local and family-backed.
She avoids AI by **choice** and gives practical reasons.
She would rather **stay near home** than chase a bigger city.

steps.text: Apply to three factories within an hour's bus ride of the village

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see what's real and what's talk. If software takes over paperwork and planning, fine, but a factory still needs people on the floor. At church I'd say honest work and skills still matter, whatever machines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not sure. The people who get hired first at plants are juniors who can set up the software and write the reports. That's the part that moves to the machines. I don't use these tools, and that might hurt me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the maintenance team for more hours with them, because hands-on skill stays valuable. I'd take a short evening apprenticeship at a local plant if one's offered, even for little pay. And I'd learn the factory's own software, but only the version they give me, nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel the ground move a little. I like clear rules and a set path, and this is neither.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why won't you use the tools, even to save time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want the work to be mine. If a program writes my report and I sign it, I can't be sure it's right. My father says that's old-fashioned. I say a signature should mean you've read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you has changed because of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Zoltan, who works in an office and uses the chat tool all day. He says it saves him two hours. I think he's right, and I can see he gets less careful with each month.

say: I'd say a factory still needs **people on the floor**.
I'd say honest work and **skills** still matter.
think: Juniors who set up software and write **reports** are hired first, and that moves to machines.
Not using the tools **might hurt** me.

Take a short evening **apprenticeship** at a local plant.
feel: I feel **anxious**, like the ground moves a little.

fieldNote: Carla's **resistance** is based on responsibility, not fear of tech.
She sees her **junior tasks** as the exposed ones.
She notices **care slipping** in her cousin Zoltan.

steps.text: Ask the factory's maintenance team for more hands-on hours

Apply for a short evening apprenticeship at a nearby plant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are not ready, and I wouldn't pretend to know what's coming. I'd ask our priest and the council to help families plan. At home I'd say pull together, grow what we can, and don't borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. The control systems I'm studying get designed by software, and in two years a machine would do my first job. The hands-on side lasts till around 2031, and I'd go there fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the search for an office job and go for a maintenance technician job, even at the lowest pay. I'd cut spending, stay with my parents and put money aside. I'd also join my grandmother and mother more on the land, because food is the thing people always need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray more than usual, and I'd be quiet at dinner. I'd try not to worry my mother, who already has her hands full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the loans mean for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve thousand in loans and a degree nobody wants. My father says he'd pay what he could from the orchard, but the orchard earns very little. I'd rather work than ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for, above all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job. Any job in a factory, near my family. People say work gives you dignity, and I believe it. I'd take a factory job sooner than a handout, even if the handout were more.

say: I'd say we're **not ready** and families should plan together.
I'd say grow what we can and **don't borrow**.
think: In two years a machine would do my **first job**.
The hands-on side lasts until about **2031**, so I'd go there fast.
do: Go for a **maintenance technician** job at the lowest pay.
Stay with my parents and put money **aside**.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, pray more than usual and stay quiet at dinner.
S2.quote: People say work gives you dignity, and I believe it. I'd take a factory job sooner than a handout, even if the handout were more.
fieldNote: Carla turns to **hands-on work** and the **family land** at once.
Her **values** (work over handouts) shape her choices even under pressure.
She hides fear to **protect** her mother.

steps.text: Apply for maintenance technician jobs at nearby plants, even at the lowest pay
Put aside most earnings while living with my parents
Stop spending on anything but the bus pass and church
Work more on the family orchard with my mother and grandmother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we begin now. At church I'd say teach the young trades and keep a bit in reserve. I'd say schools should bring back apprenticeships so graduates have a practical route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd get a job, maybe three or four years of work. It's not forever, but it's something to build on. After 2031 I don't know, and I'd rather be near family than alone in a flat in a city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any automation job near home and learn the maintenance side properly. I'd save half my pay for the first years and help my parents extend the orchard shed. I'd marry within those five years if the right person turned up, and stay in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's a clear amount of time. I think I'd feel I had room to do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about using any of the tools in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, some, yes. I'd probably try the factory's own programs, but not the free tools on the internet. I don't like depending on something I can't see inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the orchard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchard. If there's time, we could plant more trees and sell directly at the market, which is a business not a hobby. My mother says people always buy apples. I'd rather learn the numbers on it than guess.

I'd say schools should bring back **apprenticeships**.
think: I'd get **three or four years** of work, which is something to build on.
I'd rather be near **family** than alone in a city flat.

feel: I feel **anxious but steady**, with room to do things in order.
S3.quote: I'd rather be near family than alone in a flat in a city.
fieldNote: Carla values **place and family** over a bigger career.
She is **open** to company software but not free tools.
The orchard is both **identity** and a small business.

steps.text: Take the first automation job near the village and learn maintenance properly
Save half of each pay for the first three years
Stay in the village and plan a family there
Help my parents expand the orchard and sell at the market

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the young should use it to learn a skill with their hands. At church I'd say keep the faith and keep working. I'd say government should support apprenticeships, not just give handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be thirty-four, settled in the village, probably married and with children. My work would be changing, but I'd have a trade nobody can take. That feels like a comfortable place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take a maintenance job at a plant, save and help my parents. I'd learn the plant's tools when they bring them in, probably after a few years. And I'd perhaps take over part of the orchard business, since my father will be near retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, not afraid. There's a decade, and I'd have time to look after my family. I'd worry more about my younger cousins than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin Eszter, who's starting a business degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Eszter, who's starting a business degree, to learn a trade as well. If she can fix something and also understand money, she'll be fine. I'd tell her to keep a small plot of land if she can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still avoid the tools after ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If things really change in ten years, I'd have to keep up. I'd be sorry to say it, but I'd probably have to use the tools, and I'd do it once everyone around me had.

I'd say government should support **apprenticeships**, not just handouts.

I'd have time to look after my **family**.

steps.text: Work as a maintenance engineer at a nearby plant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have no time to find a place before the jobs I trained for were done. What would help is apprenticeships, work not handouts, and a church and family that stay close. I'd also want honest information from the plants about who they'll hire.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think the village is behind. It's where I grew up and it's where I'd like to stay. I don't use the tools because I'd rather understand than depend, and I'd say the same to anyone.

headlineQuote: I don't use the tools because I'd rather understand than depend, and I'd say the same to anyone.
portrait: Carla is a **24-year-old** automation engineering master's student who lives with her parents and grandmother near Debrecen.
She has a good degree, a **six-week** factory placement and about twelve thousand in loans.
Her traditional, free-market views favour **work and apprenticeships** over handouts, and she sings in the church choir.
She never uses AI and resists change, so she answers new pressure by going **hands-on** and staying near home.
She is calm in a plateau and alarmed in two years, but a **decade** lets her settle into village life.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because there'd be no time to find a place before her field's jobs went.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships**, honest hiring information from plants and a family and church that stay close.
